briefing.opening: Good morning/afternoon. We will now begin the climate briefing for August 17, 2026. Today was a day marked by severe climate disasters continuing both domestically and internationally, highlighting various efforts to respond to them, alongside policy and social challenges.

sections.title: 🔴 Extreme Climate Disasters at Home and Abroad: A Threat Becoming Reality
sections.content: Domestically today, it was reported that multi-hazards and overlapping disasters are becoming commonplace, with extreme heavy rainfall of 124mm per hour occurring after an extreme drought [2, 8, 10]. In particular, in Geoje and Tongyeong, Gyeongnam Province, landslides caused by record-breaking torrential rains followed previous extreme heatwaves, resulting in casualties and an emergency situation where national firefighting mobilization orders were issued consecutively [40, 42]. Jeju also experienced over 300mm of torrential rain in mountainous areas and over 100mm on the coast over three days, leading to reports of flood damage [44]. Internationally, the entire Northern Hemisphere is suffering from record heatwaves and climate disasters, including Europe's record June heatwave [48], droughts and wildfires in Canada's Okanagan and the UK's Dorset regions [61, 63], and casualties and evacuation orders due to fierce wildfires in France, Greece, and Belgium [67] among others, [68, 69]. These disasters threaten the daily lives of climate-vulnerable populations [41] and demonstrate that climate change is no longer a distant future concern, with even bus companies facing pressure from heatwaves [64].

sections.title: ⚠️ Administrative and Social Challenges in Responding to the Climate Crisis
sections.content: Amidst this intensifying climate crisis, concerns have been raised that climate change should not be used as a panacea to cover up administrative failures [1]. Furthermore, there is growing concern about the phenomenon of 'ecological amnesia,' where the climate crisis is easily forgotten [4], and the altered summer routines and their severity due to climate change could be overlooked [5]. In the agricultural sector, there was discussion that changes in rice farming methods are essential in the era of climate change [7]. China's '15th Five-Year Coal Plan,' which prioritizes 'energy security' over 'de-carbonization,' is expected to have significant repercussions on international climate change response efforts [9]. Domestically, difficulties persist in achieving policy consensus and setting direction, with controversies arising over the proposed amendment to the Carbon Neutrality Framework Act, accused of misleading the public [23]. Efforts to raise awareness continue, including the release of a new podcast on climate change and El Niño weather risks [51] and reporting workshops for journalists [54].

sections.title: 🌱 Diverse Domestic and International Efforts and Progress Towards a Carbon-Neutral Society
sections.content: Despite these challenges, positive movements to address climate change continue. The Korea Climate Change Research Institute is expanding carbon reduction and energy transition projects for developing countries [6], and policy efforts are ongoing, such as the re-establishment of dam design standards in response to climate change [13]. Proactive support for heatwave-vulnerable households in Seongdong-gu [14, 15] and LH's initiative to install air conditioners in new apartment elevators [43] are cited as examples of climate adaptation. Local governments like Incheon City and Gwangmyeong City are encouraging the transition to a carbon-neutral society through citizen-led carbon neutrality campaigns, the expansion of circular economy hubs, and education for future generations [18, 19, 20, 21, 24, 25, 26, 28, 29, 30]. Discussions are also underway for realizing sustainable livestock farming using data [11]. Furthermore, technological advancements are active, such as the announcement of an AI-MRV-based integrated platform for carbon neutrality and environmental analysis [32] and the successful conclusion of an eco-friendly plastics conference [31]. International efforts are also continuing, with Korea's seaweed 'Gim' finding new roles in climate change response and Oxfordshire County Council leading climate action [58, 65].

sections.title: ⚡️ Renewable Energy Transition and a Sustainable Energy Future
sections.content: Efforts to transition to renewable energy for achieving carbon neutrality are accelerating. Paju City has fully launched the supply of renewable energy to businesses using public land [34], and the Haenam solar power project is being hailed as a new milestone in renewable energy transition [35]. The government is exploring the expansion of renewable energy supply by reviewing the easing of regulations for building-integrated photovoltaics, and business agreements related to eco-friendly energy are being actively concluded [36, 39]. However, concerns have been raised that the generation cost of wind and solar power could increase if system costs are reflected [38], necessitating consideration for establishing efficient and stable renewable energy systems. Internationally, Egypt is demonstrating its commitment to transition by setting a target of 45% renewable energy by 2028, even as it records its highest-ever electricity demand [33]. AUKUS is proposing nuclear solutions for climate change to Australia, sparking diverse discussions on the energy mix [52]. There are also calls for South Korea's energy Official Development Assistance (ODA) approach to shift from simply constructing solar power plants to 'package exports' [37].

briefing.closing: As you have seen in today's briefing, climate change is now having immediate and complex impacts across our daily lives and society as a whole. To overcome this crisis and build a sustainable future, global efforts are crucial, and it is paramount that each of us takes climate action in our respective roles. This concludes the climate briefing for August 17, 2026.
